items.readable_text:
Content:
In this topic, we'll study phase portraits of linear systems
[MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]
where the [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix [MATH: A] has a repeated real eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda] (algebraic multiplicity [MATH: 2]).

Content:
If [MATH: A] has two independent eigenvectors, then [MATH: A] is the scalar matrix
[MATH: [λ|0; 0|λ]]
In this case, every direction through the origin behaves like an eigenvector direction, and trajectories are straight lines:
[MATH: \mathbf{x}(t)=e^{\lambda t} \mathbf{v}, \qquad \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^2.]

Content:
So the phase portrait is a star node:

Content:
- If [MATH: \lambda>0,] trajectories move away from the origin and we have an unstable star node.
- If [MATH: \lambda<0,] trajectories move toward the origin and we have a stable star node.

Content:
Let's see an example.

Content:
Let's sketch the phase portrait of the following linear system:

Content:
[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = 2x(t); y^{′}(t) = 2y(t)]

Content:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have
[MATH: [2|0; 0|2]]
where [MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]

Content:
Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are [MATH: \lambda_1=\lambda_2=2] with the corresponding eigenvectors [MATH: [1; 0]] and [MATH: [0; 1]]

Content:
The general solution of the system is
[MATH: [1; 0]]

Content:
Notice that for each vector [MATH: [c_{1}; c_{2}]] we get the straight-line solutions of the form
[MATH: [c_{1}; c_{2}]]
that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector [MATH: [c_{1}; c_{2}]]

Content:
Since [MATH: e^{2t} \to \infty] as [MATH: t \to \infty,] these solutions move away from the origin as [MATH: t \to \infty,] so the origin is an unstable node.

[MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]
where the [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix [MATH: A] has a repeated real eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda] (algebraic multiplicity [MATH: 2]).

[MATH: (A-\lambda I)\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{v},]

[MATH: \mathbf{x}(t)=c_1 e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}+c_2 e^{\lambda t}\bigl(t\,\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}\bigr).]
Here, the eigenvector line (the line through the origin parallel to [MATH: \mathbf{v}]) is still a straight-line solution, but other trajectories are curved and become tangent to that eigenvector line.

Content:
In cases like this, the phase portrait is a degenerate node:

Content:

- If [MATH: \lambda<0,] trajectories move toward the origin and we have a stable degenerate node.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this topic, we'll study phase portraits of linear systems
[MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]
where the [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix [MATH: A] has a repeated real eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda] (algebraic multiplicity [MATH: 2]).

Content:
If [MATH: A] has two independent eigenvectors, then [MATH: A] is the scalar matrix
[MATH: [λ|0; 0|λ]]
In this case, every direction through the origin behaves like an eigenvector direction, and trajectories are straight lines:
[MATH: \mathbf{x}(t)=e^{\lambda t} \mathbf{v}, \qquad \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^2.]

Content:
So the phase portrait is a star node:

Content:
- If [MATH: \lambda>0,] trajectories move away from the origin and we have an unstable star node.
- If [MATH: \lambda<0,] trajectories move toward the origin and we have a stable star node.

Content:
Let's see an example.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: A Worked Example of a Star Node

Content:
Let's sketch the phase portrait of the following linear system:

Content:
[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = 2x(t); y^{′}(t) = 2y(t)]

Content:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have
[MATH: [2|0; 0|2]]
where [MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]

Content:
Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are [MATH: \lambda_1=\lambda_2=2] with the corresponding eigenvectors [MATH: [1; 0]] and [MATH: [0; 1]]

Content:
The general solution of the system is
[MATH: [1; 0]]

Content:
Notice that for each vector [MATH: [c_{1}; c_{2}]] we get the straight-line solutions of the form
[MATH: [c_{1}; c_{2}]]
that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector [MATH: [c_{1}; c_{2}]]

Content:
Since [MATH: e^{2t} \to \infty] as [MATH: t \to \infty,] these solutions move away from the origin as [MATH: t \to \infty,] so the origin is an unstable node.

Content:
The phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/319549b6079de68ca9f6fa8445d65a74]

---

Item 3 — Example: Identifying the Phase Portrait of a Decoupled System With Repeated Eigenvalues

Example Prompt:
[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = − 8x(t); y^{′}(t) = − 8y(t)]
Sketch the phase portrait of the linear system above.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have
[MATH: [− 8|0; 0|− 8]]
where [MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are [MATH: \lambda_1=\lambda_2=-8] with the corresponding eigenvectors [MATH: [1; 0]] and [MATH: [0; 1]]

The general solution of the system is
[MATH: [1; 0]]

Notice that for each vector [MATH: [c_{1}; c_{2}]] we get the straight-line solutions of the form
[MATH: [c_{1}; c_{2}]]
that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector [MATH: [c_{1}; c_{2}]]

Since [MATH: e^{-8t} \to 0] as [MATH: t \to \infty,] these solutions approach the origin as [MATH: t \to \infty,] so the origin is a stable node.

The phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

[IMG: /graphics/24987f26ca917591ec4d8c2ddbbf8735]

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: Systems With Repeated Eigenvalues

Content:
Recall that in this topic, we're studying phase portraits of linear systems
[MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]
where the [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix [MATH: A] has a repeated real eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda] (algebraic multiplicity [MATH: 2]).

Content:
If [MATH: A] has only one eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf{v},] and if [MATH: \mathbf{w}] is a generalized eigenvector satisfying
[MATH: (A-\lambda I)\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{v},]
then the general solution takes the form
[MATH: \mathbf{x}(t)=c_1 e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}+c_2 e^{\lambda t}\bigl(t\,\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}\bigr).]
Here, the eigenvector line (the line through the origin parallel to [MATH: \mathbf{v}]) is still a straight-line solution, but other trajectories are curved and become tangent to that eigenvector line.

Content:
In cases like this, the phase portrait is a degenerate node:

Content:
- If [MATH: \lambda>0,] trajectories move away from the origin and we have an unstable degenerate node.
- If [MATH: \lambda<0,] trajectories move toward the origin and we have a stable degenerate node.

Content:
Let's see an example.

---

In our case,

Thus, the general solution of the system is

The straight-line solutions of the form
